issues.legal_issue: A consent decree recognizing a family-settlement claim to property that was the subject matter of the suit does not require registration where it acknowledges a pre-existing right.
material_facts: The suit concerned the disputed land, and the decree followed the landowner’s admission of the claimant’s claim.
The landowner testified that part of the land was ancestral, and the Court found that this portion came to the claimant under a family settlement.
The Court treated the decree as acknowledging the claimant’s entitlement to that portion under the family settlement, rather than as creating a new right by gift.
issues.conclusion: The decree concerning the portion transferred under the family settlement did not require compulsory registration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, 1908 exempts a court decree concerning property that is the subject matter of the suit from the relevant registration requirement. The Court applied the distinction discussed in Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major, (1995) 5 SCC 709, and K. Raghunandan v. Ali Hussain Sabir, (2008) 13 SCC 102; a three-judge Bench had found no inconsistency between those decisions. A decree acknowledging a pre-existing right under a family settlement is distinct from one creating a new right in the property for the first time.

predicates.consent_decree_dispute: The dispute concerns a consent decree that determines rights in property.
predicates.property_was_suit_subject_matter: The property addressed by the decree was included in the suit.
predicates.decree_acknowledges_preexisting_settleme: The decree recognizes a claim to the property under a family settlement rather than creating a new right by transfer.

issues.definition: When a consent decree concerns property included in the suit and recognizes a pre-existing right under a family settlement, the decree need not be registered.

issues.legal_issue: A gift that creates an interest in immovable property for the first time requires compulsory registration even when a court decree is also made concerning the property.
material_facts: The landowner testified that part of the disputed land had been purchased by him and was his self-acquired property.
The Court found that he had gifted this portion to the claimant of his own free will, thereby creating the claimant’s interest in that portion for the first time.
The value of the immovable property exceeded the registration threshold.
issues.conclusion: The gift of the self-acquired portion required compulsory registration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(a) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires registration of an instrument that effects a gift of immovable property of the relevant value. Applying Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major, (1995) 5 SCC 709, the Court held that a decree does not remove the registration requirement where the transfer creates a right, title or interest in the property for the first time. This differs from the treatment of the portion recognized under the family settlement under Section 17(2)(vi).

rule.if: property_transfer_dispute and transfer_is_gift and gift_creates_first_time_interest and immovable_property_exceeds_registration_threshold

predicates.property_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns the transfer of rights in immovable property.
predicates.transfer_is_gift: The owner gave the property to another person as a gift.
predicates.gift_creates_first_time_interest: The gift created the recipient’s right in the property for the first time.
predicates.immovable_property_exceeds_registration_: The value of the immovable property is above the threshold at which registration is required.

issues.definition: If a gift in a property-transfer dispute creates an interest in immovable property for the first time and the property exceeds the registration threshold, the gift requires compulsory registration.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot challenge the validity of a gift for the first time in a final appeal when the challenge has no foundation in the pleadings, issues or evidence.
material_facts: The parties seeking to challenge the gift had not pleaded a challenge to its validity in the suit.
No issue concerning the validity of the gift had been framed.
No evidence had been led to challenge the gift’s validity.
The challenge was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the challenge to the gift’s validity for the first time in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot decide a newly raised challenge to a transaction when no factual foundation for it was laid in the pleadings, no issue was framed, and no evidence was led. The Court did not rely on a specific statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: final_appeal and gift_validity_challenged_for_first_time and challenge_not_pleaded and no_issue_framed and no_evidence_supports_challenge

predicates.final_appeal: The proceeding is a final appeal from a lower-court decision.
predicates.gift_validity_challenged_for_first_time: A party first contests the validity of a gift in the final appeal.
predicates.challenge_not_pleaded: The party did not plead the validity challenge in the underlying suit.
predicates.no_issue_framed: The lower court did not frame an issue on the validity challenge.
predicates.no_evidence_supports_challenge: The party led no evidence in the lower court to support the validity challenge.

issues.definition: In a final appeal, a first-time challenge to a gift is not entertained when it was not pleaded, no issue was framed, and no supporting evidence was led.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that a consent decree was not collusive cannot be reopened in the same appeal after the Supreme Court has already settled that finding.
material_facts: The first appellate court had found that the consent decree was not collusive.
In an earlier order in the same appeal, the Supreme Court held that the finding of non-collusion could not be disturbed.
A three-judge Bench subsequently concluded that there was no inconsistency between the earlier decisions that had prompted referral, and the appeal returned for decision on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not reopen the finding that the consent decree was not collusive.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated its prior determination in the same appeal that the decree was not collusive as settled and binding for the appeal’s later consideration. It also treated the three-judge Bench’s conclusion that there was no inconsistency between Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major, (1995) 5 SCC 709, and K. Raghunandan v. Ali Hussain Sabir, (2008) 13 SCC 102, as closing the referred question.

predicates.same_appeal: The later proceeding is the continuation of the same appeal.
predicates.prior_supreme_court_order_resolved_collu: An earlier Supreme Court order in the appeal settled whether the decree was collusive.
predicates.later_consideration_follows_that_order: The Court is considering the appeal after the earlier order and no basis is given to reopen its determination.

issues.definition: When an earlier Supreme Court order in the same appeal has resolved the collusion issue, that finding is not reopened in the appeal’s later consideration.
